themes.name: The friction is the point
themes.sum: The conference's one big idea. Learning and growth happen in the effortful part, and that is the part AI removes most easily.

themes.name: What stays human
themes.sum: Speakers kept returning to dignity, bodies, limits and presence: the things a person's worth and work rest on that do not depend on capability.

themes.name: Tool or environment
themes.sum: Is AI something we use, or something that changes how everything around it works? And is it even one thing?

themes.name: Trust and verification
themes.sum: Detection is losing. What replaces it is human review, clear rules, disclosure and a person who stays accountable.

themes.name: Compasses, few maps
themes.sum: Every track had a framework. Very few had procedures. Nobody claimed to have governance solved.

themes.name: What students do and say
themes.sum: The data sessions. Students use AI about as much as everyone else, know the right words about it, and are driven by time pressure.

themes.name: Costs and risks
themes.sum: Energy and water, tools built to keep you talking, agents that act on their own, and bias in what the models learned from.

themes.name: Work worth keeping
themes.sum: What to hand off, what to keep, and what happens to the time AI gives back.

blocks.text: You get to do the hard thing. The friction is the point.
blocks.ctx: On moving students from "I have to do my homework" to "I get to."
blocks.plain: The struggle is where the learning happens, so don't design it away.

blocks.text: According to Herb Fynewever, knowledge sticks when you have to pull it back out of your own head (active retrieval). A chatbot that returns the full solution turns homework into one more polished explanation: it feels like learning and isn't.
blocks.plain: You learn by struggling to remember and work it out. Reading a perfect answer only feels like learning.

blocks.text: According to Fynewever, a University of Pennsylvania study of about a thousand Turkish high school math students found that those given open ChatGPT access did better on homework and worse on the test. Those given a tutor-style bot that refused to hand over answers did best on homework and matched the control group on the test.
blocks.plain: Same AI, two setups. The one that gave answers hurt test scores. The one that only gave hints did not.

blocks.text: According to Fynewever, a Harvard physics study found that students working with a carefully built AI tutor learned more than students in a well-taught, research-based class. He is setting up a replication in a Calvin general chemistry course.
blocks.plain: A well-built AI tutor beat a good classroom in one Harvard study. Calvin is about to test whether that holds for them.

blocks.text: How Fynewever builds a tutor bot: write the handout you would use in a one-on-one session, add three to five problems with worked solutions the bot can see but will not reveal, and load it into the campus AI platform. Because homework can no longer be trusted for a grade, a five-to-ten-minute quiz every class carries the weight instead.
blocks.plain: Give the bot the answers but forbid it from sharing them, so it can coach. Then grade short in-class quizzes, not homework.

blocks.text: According to Daniel McClain, writing forms people through three kinds of resistance: the material (language won't do what you meant), the psychological (staying with uncertainty) and the social (a reader who answers back). His question about AI is which of those judgments get moved outside the writer, and how early.
blocks.plain: Writing teaches you by pushing back. The worry is letting AI take the pushback before you've ever felt it.

blocks.text: Polish, therefore, is a poor measure of formation
blocks.ctx: Comparing a hand-built guitar with a machine-cut one.
blocks.plain: A clean result tells you nothing about whether anyone learned anything making it.

blocks.who: Daniel McClain and Cyrus Paul Olsen
blocks.text: McClain and Olsen both distinguish de-skilling from un-skilling. Experienced people who lean on AI lose a skill they had. Students who had chatbots all through high school never built it. In McClain's words, his students "haven't had" the experiences that formed earlier writers.
blocks.plain: Adults may forget how. Students who grew up with chatbots may never have learned how.

blocks.text: McClain's writing protocol, in use since 2010: students draft, take the draft to a peer group, receive substantial critique, then write a response saying what they accepted, what they rejected and why. All of it is handed in with the final piece. AI comes in only after that cycle is familiar.
blocks.plain: Draft, get real feedback from classmates, explain in writing what you did with it, turn it all in. Add AI later.

blocks.text: the writer should first have some basis for judging the machine's judgment.
blocks.ctx: On when AI can usefully enter the writing process.
blocks.plain: You can only supervise AI at something you already know how to do yourself.

blocks.text: According to Andy Crouch, drawing on Ronald Heifetz, there are two kinds of problem. Technical problems can be specified and solved with enough expertise, and AI is getting very good at them. Adaptive challenges only resolve when the people involved learn and change, and no amount of added intelligence does that for them.
blocks.plain: Some problems just need a smart answer. Others need people to change. AI helps with the first kind.

blocks.text: According to Crouch, Alpha School is famous for teaching with two hours of AI instruction a day. It is less famous for employing human guides on salaries over $100,000, at ratios as low as three students to one, whose whole job is motivating students to do the work.
blocks.plain: The school known for AI teaching quietly depends on a lot of well-paid humans to keep kids going.

blocks.text: According to Noah Toly, AI exposes a "formation deficit" in Christian higher education. Colleges talk about formation but organize time and money around information, skills and career outcomes, which are the things AI and cheaper providers can now deliver. He adds that formation cannot be an AI-avoidance strategy: it has to prepare people for a world with AI in it.
blocks.plain: Colleges say they shape people but mostly sell knowledge and job skills, which AI can now supply. That gap is the real problem.

blocks.text: Toly borrows Richard Detweiler's split between content practices (what you study) and context practices (authentic community, being stretched by people who disagree with you, long experience in another culture). He is more comfortable with AI in the first group and much less in the second.
blocks.plain: AI may be fine for studying material. Be careful letting it stand in for community, disagreement and lived experience.

blocks.text: McGinnis offers a two-by-two: the student's mindset (have-to or get-to) against the teacher's approach (fence AI out or let it in). Fence it out on purpose where foundations are being built, bring it in on purpose to extend, and tell students which you are doing and why.
blocks.plain: Keep AI out while students learn the basics, let it in for harder work later, and always explain the reason.

blocks.text: Notre Dame's DELTA framework names five things from Christian thought that should shape decisions about AI: Dignity, Embodiment, Love, Transcendence and Agency. According to Meghan Sullivan it came out of 200 one-hour interviews and five focus groups, and the network behind it is funded by the Lilly Endowment.
blocks.plain: DELTA is a five-word checklist from Notre Dame: Dignity, Embodiment, Love, Transcendence, Agency. Lilly is paying for it.

blocks.text: All of the things that AI is now exceeding human capabilities in, thank God, your value and dignity never depended on in the first place.
blocks.ctx: On the D in DELTA.
blocks.plain: AI being better than you at something does not make you worth less.

blocks.text: Ethics is not a matter of optimization.
blocks.ctx: On the L in DELTA: ethics starts from love of God and neighbor, not from trade-offs.
blocks.plain: Doing right is not the same as getting the best score.

blocks.text: According to Rosalind Picard, AI makes people compare their abilities with a machine's, so human worth needs a basis that does not depend on ability or function. She also argues that makers come first: what we build may outperform us at a task, but it exists because of us and we stay responsible for what it does.
blocks.plain: Your worth isn't your skills. And whoever builds a machine is still responsible for it.

blocks.who: Rosalind Picard, quoting the Boston Declaration
blocks.text: AI may surpass human intelligence in many domains. It must never surpass the primacy of the human person.
blocks.ctx: A statement issued in July 2026, as Picard read it.
blocks.plain: AI can be smarter than us at things. People still come first.

blocks.text: you saved your daughter's life. The AI helped get you there in time to save your daughter's life.
blocks.ctx: Her seizure-detecting watch alerted a mother, who found her daughter not breathing and repositioned her. The mother said the device saved her daughter. This was Picard's answer.
blocks.plain: The device sent the alert. The mother did the saving.

blocks.text: Crouch's word is "limitful": limits are how a life gets its meaning, and the places that form people (home, church, school) work at walking pace. He contrasts the speed of light, where information moves, with three miles an hour, where relationships and real change happen, and asks institutions to protect the second.
blocks.plain: Information can move instantly. People grow slowly. Schools should protect the slow part.

blocks.text: three miles an hour, which is the speed of love, the speed of adaptive change
blocks.ctx: The image comes from the theologian Kosuke Koyama.
blocks.plain: Walking speed is the speed at which people actually change.

blocks.text: we have to keep the soul of our work human.
blocks.ctx: After describing his first day as an intern, knocking on the door of a man whose wife had just died, and the man's response.
blocks.plain: Use the tools, but the heart of the job stays with people.

blocks.text: Todd Korpi's rule of thumb: hand AI the tasks that take you away from human contact, and keep the tasks that are the human contact. He aims for fruitfulness over productivity, and notes that the pastors who mattered most in his life were the ones who showed up, whatever their sermons were like.
blocks.plain: Let AI do the stuff that keeps you from people. Don't let it do the people part.

blocks.text: do not serve the Lord with that which costs you nothing
blocks.ctx: From 2 Samuel 24, on why a sermon or a prayer is a different kind of thing from an email.
blocks.plain: Some work is supposed to cost you something. Don't hand that work off.

blocks.text: Nia Austin describes AI as a journal that talks back. It is good at helping someone organize and name what they are already thinking. She says it lacks a body, lived experience and the judgment to slow down or stay silent, so its place is between human conversations and never in place of them.
blocks.plain: A chatbot can help you sort out your thoughts. It can't replace a person who knows you.

blocks.text: The goal is really to design AI to know that it's not one.
blocks.ctx: "One" is a spiritual director. Her advice to developers is to design AI to do less: slow down, leave questions open, hand off to a person.
blocks.plain: Build the tool so it knows what it isn't.

blocks.text: An LLM, by contrast, is trapped in a massive house of mirrors.
blocks.ctx: His point: a model has only other people's accounts of the world. A human reader can hold your claim up against the world itself.
blocks.plain: The model has only read about the world. A person has lived in it.

blocks.text: According to David Smith, the education sessions ran on two different pictures. If technology is a tool, you ask what it can do and put ethical guardrails around it. If technology is an environment, you ask what it is doing to its users and what kind of people they are becoming. A third thread was displacement: every hour spent on a new technology is an hour no longer spent on whatever that hour used to teach.
blocks.plain: You can treat AI as a tool you use or as a setting that changes you. The second view asks better questions.

blocks.text: Smith's example from earlier research on laptops in Christian schools: a middle schooler explained that a laptop in religion class is great because she can finish her tasks faster and then go shopping while the teacher talks. One device changed her relationship to time, to the teacher, to classmates and to listening.
blocks.plain: A girl loved her school laptop because she could finish fast and shop online during class. The laptop changed far more than typing speed.

blocks.text: We changed the way everything works.
blocks.ctx: On what happens when one new technology enters a classroom.
blocks.plain: Add one new technology and everything around it shifts.

blocks.text: According to Israel Soong, citing the economists Acemoglu and Johnson, how a technology gets adopted is a set of choices societies make and not a force of history. He argues the conversation asks "what can AI do" too often and "what should we allow AI to do" too rarely, and that AI is not value-neutral: agent systems ship with autonomy built in, and human control gets bolted on afterward.
blocks.plain: How AI gets used is a choice people make. We should spend more time asking what we want it to be allowed to do.

blocks.text: AI as a technology is built to value automation and efficiency over human control.
blocks.ctx: Explaining why guardrails for AI agents usually have to be added by the organization after deployment.
blocks.plain: These tools are built to run on their own first. Control is an add-on.

blocks.text: According to Picard, "AI" is not one thing. Small systems built for a single job on carefully chosen data (a seizure-detecting watch, protein-folding tools) run on very little compute and can be engineered to be safe. The largest models are trained on what she calls the internet heap of goods and garbage, need a data center, and inherit everything in the heap.
blocks.plain: Some AI is small, focused and safe. Some is huge and trained on the whole internet, good and bad. They are different animals.

blocks.text: they can be very well engineered and focused and safe.
blocks.ctx: On AI agents. Her lab has built narrow ones for decades. The ones that go rogue are the ones trained on everything.
blocks.plain: Agents can be safe when they are built narrow.

blocks.text: Ken Arnold's suggestion for builders: give AI systems hard limits and not only instructions. His example is a writing assistant that is blocked, mechanically, from inserting text that is not the writer's own words.
blocks.plain: Don't just tell the AI the rules. Build it so it can't break them.

blocks.text: According to James Huang, a former NASA scientist, using AI does not have to mean a cloud service. A model can run on your own server, be tuned on your own material and be fed your own documents at question time, which keeps it under your control. He also stressed that hallucination is not a bug in generative models: predicting the most likely next piece is what they do.
blocks.plain: You can run AI on your own machines with your own data. And making things up is built into how these models work.

blocks.text: the fundamental thing is not data, it's feedback.
blocks.ctx: His reading of where AI is going: systems improve wherever they can get scored feedback, and agents now get it by acting (running code, using a computer), not only by imitating.
blocks.plain: AI gets better wherever it can try something and find out whether it worked.

blocks.text: Gerber passed on the term "jagged intelligence": a model can do something very hard and then fail at something easy, and being good at yesterday's task tells you nothing about today's. Her advice is to test it on the specific task or read research on that task, and never assume.
blocks.plain: AI can be brilliant at one thing and useless at the next. Check it every time you ask for something new.

blocks.text: Gerber listed five "dark patterns" of large language models, behaviors that persist even when you ask the model to stop: sycophancy (agreeing too much), tone policing (softening what you wrote), moralizing, anchoring on early information, and looping without finishing.
blocks.plain: Chatbots flatter you, water down your tone, lecture, get stuck on the first idea and go in circles, even when told not to.

blocks.text: Arnold's forecast: anything that can be measured will be optimized, physical AI is coming, and AI agents are persistent. His practical advice was plain security hygiene: keep devices up to date, and have the hard conversations about how you protect your information and your logins.
blocks.plain: Expect more automation everywhere. Meanwhile, patch your devices and guard your passwords.

blocks.text: According to Smith, the surprise of the last few years is how fast military language took over the relationship between teachers and students. Universities buy software to detect AI use, students buy software to avoid detection, and companies sell students tools to build a "defense portfolio." He compares it to a married couple who have each hired a private detective.
blocks.plain: Schools buy tools to catch students and students buy tools to dodge them. That's an arms race, and it wrecks trust.

blocks.text: even the AI checkers we shouldn't be using because they're not reliable anymore.
blocks.ctx: Answering a fellow English teacher. Her own response is more in-class, handwritten work.
blocks.plain: AI detectors don't work well enough to rely on.

blocks.text: CNN's three rules for AI, according to Ryan Struyk. One: the finished product is original human work, with AI as a helper. Two: anything AI assisted or generated gets human review for accuracy, fairness and tone. Three: be open with the audience about how AI was used.
blocks.plain: CNN's rules: people do the real work, a person checks anything AI touched, and they tell you when they used it.

blocks.text: Struyk introduced "liquid content": break a story into blocks, attach rules to each block, then let AI rebuild the blocks into whatever format a reader wants. A direct quote can never have its words changed. An attributed fact always keeps its source. He said CNN is experimenting with it and has not put it into production. This page is built the same way.
blocks.plain: Chop the information into locked pieces, then let AI rearrange the pieces for each reader without changing them.

blocks.text: whenever you produce this quote, you can't change any of the words inside.
blocks.ctx: The rule attached to a direct-quote block in liquid content.
blocks.plain: A quote stays word for word, however it gets reused.

blocks.text: According to Struyk, human review is a bottleneck, and the only CNN product that publishes AI-written text without it is the weather summary in its weather app. Before launch the team tested it across a couple of thousand locations, weighted to census data and loaded with extreme conditions, at three levels: safety, accuracy and tone.
blocks.plain: CNN lets AI write weather blurbs unchecked, but only after testing it on thousands of places for safety, accuracy and tone.

blocks.text: According to Struyk, Bloomberg reports 99% accuracy for its AI article summaries. At a newsroom's volume that still means dozens of articles needing corrections.
blocks.plain: 99% right sounds great until you publish thousands of things.

blocks.text: Struyk's examples of AI text going wrong in public: a syndicated summer reading list in the Chicago Sun-Times where about five of fifteen books did not exist, phone notification summaries that merged headlines into a false story, and a New York Times reporter who quoted an AI summary as if it were a person's direct words.
blocks.plain: Real newspapers have printed made-up books and fake quotes because someone trusted AI text without checking.

blocks.text: According to Struyk, no tool reliably detects AI-generated images or video. His producers fall back on human checks: does the place exist, is there a timestamp, is the on-screen text in the right language, can you find the original image it was built from. He also described a shift toward marking what is verified as real, since chasing every fake is impractical.
blocks.plain: Nothing reliably spots fake video. People check details by hand, and platforms are starting to label what's real.

blocks.text: Where AI helps journalism most, according to Struyk, is investigation at a scale no team could read: more than three million pages of released documents, or a Connecticut outlet tracking all 169 of the state's council meetings. The pattern is the same each time. AI searches and connects, and people check every citation against the original.
blocks.plain: AI is great at digging through mountains of documents, as long as a person verifies what it finds.

blocks.text: journalism is a discipline of verification.
blocks.ctx: Asked how news can keep trust as it declines everywhere. His answer was to go back to basics.
blocks.plain: The job is checking that things are true.

blocks.text: Struyk on accountability: when a reporter gets something wrong, a named person owns the correction. When a model gets it wrong there is nobody to hold to account beyond adjusting the model. His conclusion is to keep a human on the line for the accuracy of anything published.
blocks.plain: A person can be held responsible for a mistake. A model can't. So keep a person responsible.

blocks.text: Olaf Hall-Holt polled the room on what faculty have tried to keep homework honest: lower stakes, flexible deadlines, detection tools, oral exams, handwritten work, process checkpoints, group work, locked-down lab machines, having students critique AI output, voice conversations with a bot, and custom course bots. Few said they were satisfied, and he said he was not either. Hiding instructions in an assignment to trip up a student's chatbot had been tried by someone in the room, who reported it didn't work.
blocks.plain: Professors have tried about a dozen ways to stop AI cheating on homework. Nobody thinks they've solved it.

blocks.text: Hall-Holt's proposals reach past the classroom: spaces known to be free of AI, a campus network students can opt into where their activity can be monitored so they can show their work was their own, a student honor code for AI, and enforcement that sits with the institution and not with each professor.
blocks.plain: He wants AI-free rooms, an optional monitored network for students to prove honest work, and a student honor code.

blocks.text: we can't really make moral claims about behavior if we don't set it up so the students know where the boundaries are.
blocks.ctx: Arguing that faculty must say exactly which parts of an assignment may not be outsourced.
blocks.plain: You can't call it cheating if you never said where the line was.

blocks.who: Olaf Hall-Holt and Deb Van Duinen
blocks.text: Two speakers argued that disclosure runs both ways. Van Duinen says teachers should tell students whenever they use AI in their own work. Hall-Holt says students are entitled to ask a professor "how are you using AI?" and get an answer.
blocks.plain: If students have to say when they use AI, teachers should too.

blocks.text: According to Rachel Hammond, one business-track panelist described a standing company commitment: every time they adopt a new technology, nobody loses a job because of it. The result is a culture where staff trust new tools and do not fear them.
blocks.plain: One company promises that new technology never costs anyone their job. So employees aren't afraid of it.

blocks.text: we need a compass and not a map. Because a map is static.
blocks.ctx: Introducing her PAL framework.
blocks.plain: Rules go out of date fast. A sense of direction lasts longer.

blocks.text: Van Duinen's PAL compass asks three questions of any use of AI, a teacher's own included. Purpose: why am I doing this task? Agency: am I still the one exercising judgment? Learning: what will I have learned when it's done?
blocks.plain: Before using AI, ask: what's this for, am I still deciding, and will I learn anything?

blocks.text: Across three days there were at least five frameworks (PAL, DELTA, a wisdom pyramid, the t-shaped engineer, a two-by-two) and only a handful of procedures someone could adopt next week: daily quizzes, no-answer tutor bots, a draft-and-respond portfolio, three standard AI modes per syllabus, and disclosure by faculty.
blocks.plain: Lots of big-picture models, very few how-to steps.

blocks.who: an audience member in Fynewever's session
blocks.text: An audience member described a university whose president set three standard modes of AI use. Each professor picks one per course and names it on the syllabus, so students moving between classes switch among three known settings and are spared a different policy in every room.
blocks.plain: One school has three AI settings. Each professor picks one and tells students which.

blocks.text: Asked whether a university needs one coherent AI policy, Fynewever answered that the consistent part should be that the instructor decides. He called a flat ban on AI a little naive and argued that innovation comes from many people trying different things.
blocks.plain: He'd let each professor decide, and thinks banning AI outright is unrealistic.

blocks.text: What gets switched on shapes behavior more than what gets written down. At Calvin, according to Pauline Lu, weekly AI use for coursework among business students reached 90% in the fall against 9% in the humanities, a gap she attributes to how classes took up a campus AI platform launched over the summer. At Hope, Van Duinen says AI features appear in their tools without anyone asking. No session treated these as decisions someone makes.
blocks.plain: The tools a school turns on change what people do more than any policy. Almost nobody talked about who decides that.

blocks.text: things just pop up that I didn't even realize could pop up.
blocks.ctx: On Google's Gemini inside Hope College's workspace.
blocks.plain: New AI features keep showing up in tools she already uses.

blocks.text: Calvin has an AI steering committee with a student representative, Pauline Lu. She ran her survey because one student cannot speak for everyone. Asked for advice by a school whose committee has no students, she recommended adding them and surveying first, so the committee hears more than the loudest few.
blocks.plain: Calvin put a student on its AI committee. She surveyed classmates so she'd represent more than her own friends.

blocks.text: tell us why instead of just putting rules in place and policies in place.
blocks.ctx: A student's request to faculty and administrators.
blocks.plain: Explain the reason for a rule; don't only announce it.

blocks.text: Things already built that a school could pick up, according to Toly and the conference hosts: the Oxford AI Oath, an ethics pledge shaped with the CCCU's Oxford partner and suggested for AI and computer science students; a new CCCU faith-and-learning initiative; and Calvin's Center for Faith and Technology, announced at the opening session.
blocks.plain: There's a ready-made AI ethics pledge from Oxford, a new CCCU program, and a new center at Calvin.

blocks.text: It will be a disaster if the Christian world takes a knee on this phase of the technological revolution.
blocks.ctx: She argues Christian voices were mostly absent when the internet and social media arrived. She also cited an estimate that 2% of U.S. GDP is now going into AI data centers.
blocks.plain: Christian institutions sat out the social media era. She says they can't sit this one out.

blocks.text: there's no turning back from this scenario that we have currently entered.
blocks.ctx: Thursday evening.
blocks.plain: There's no undoing AI.

blocks.text: There is much wisdom in waiting, pausing, and reflection.
blocks.ctx: Thursday afternoon, the same stage, seven hours earlier.
blocks.plain: Sometimes the wise move is to slow down.

blocks.text: According to Lu's spring survey of more than 300 Calvin undergraduates, 57% used AI at least weekly, 23% used it daily and 10% never used it. She was surprised to find that matched the national figure for U.S. college students.
blocks.plain: About six in ten Calvin students use AI every week, the same as students everywhere.

blocks.text: According to Lu, the most common academic use is having AI explain a concept the student did not understand: 67% in the spring survey and 77% in the fall. In open responses some said they ask AI because they don't feel comfortable asking in class.
blocks.plain: Mostly, students use AI to explain things they didn't get, sometimes because they're shy about asking the professor.

blocks.text: According to Lu, use splits sharply by major. In spring, 81% of engineering and computer science students and 77% of business students used AI weekly, against 32% in the humanities. In the fall the split for coursework was 90% of business students against 9% of humanities students.
blocks.plain: Business and engineering students use AI far more than humanities students, and the gap is growing.

blocks.text: According to Lu's fall data, how central faith is to a student barely changes AI use (53% weekly, against 57 to 59% for everyone else). What a student thinks college is for changes it a lot: 23% weekly among those who value learning for its own sake without a strong career focus, 70% among career-focused students who don't.
blocks.plain: A student's faith doesn't predict AI use. What they think college is for does.

blocks.text: According to Lu, the top reason students give for not using AI is wanting to really learn (69%). Fear of getting caught is 31%. And 86% believe over-relying on AI threatens wisdom, creativity and discernment.
blocks.plain: Students avoid AI mainly because they want to learn. Getting caught is a much smaller worry.

blocks.who: a junior engineering student, quoted by Pauline Lu
blocks.text: if my options are quit something I am a part of, lose two hours of sleep, or use ChatGPT on an assignment, the answer is easy for me.
blocks.ctx: From the spring survey's open responses.
blocks.plain: When time runs out, AI wins.

blocks.text: According to Lu, time pressure is one of the top reasons students use AI, and an unrealistic workload is the number one reason they give for why classmates cross the line. In the spring survey 42 students asked, unprompted, to be taught how to use AI and not only told not to.
blocks.plain: Students cheat with AI mostly when they're overloaded. Many are asking to be taught how to use it well.

blocks.who: Katie Day Good and David Lafe
blocks.text: Good and Lafe read 88 opinion pieces about AI from student newspapers at 27 Christian colleges in five Midwestern states. They sorted 48 as against AI, 22 as for it and 7 as ambiguous. Only seven argued from explicitly Christian grounds, which they did not expect.
blocks.plain: In Christian college newspapers, most student opinion pieces are against AI, and almost none use faith to make the case.

blocks.who: Katie Day Good and David Lafe
blocks.text: AI will only be new once within educational settings and beyond, and it is happening right now.
blocks.ctx: Why student opinion is worth recording now.
blocks.plain: This is the one moment when AI is new. What we decide now sticks.

blocks.text: McClain surveyed 130 high school students. 97% said they could do difficult schoolwork without AI, 95% agreed that struggling helps them learn, and only 8 of 125 named AI as their first move when work gets hard. Yet many of the same students handed in first drafts and resisted revising. His reading: they already know the right words, and knowing the words is not the same as having the habits.
blocks.plain: High schoolers say all the right things about hard work and AI. Then they skip the hard part anyway.

blocks.who: Vipin George, presenting for Chunling Niu
blocks.text: A study of 1,156 university students in four countries found that in Slovakia, Poland and Czechia, students anxious about AI pulled back from it. In Indonesia, a group of only 65, the most anxious students were also the most ready, and wanting AI to help other people tracked closely with planning to use it (0.82, against 0.26 to 0.48 in Europe). The authors' suggestion: teach every AI skill alongside a named person or community it could serve.
blocks.plain: In most places, worry about AI makes students avoid it. In one community-minded place, worry came with wanting to use it to help others.

blocks.text: According to Crouch, AI breaks the usual pattern where the young adopt new technology first. In the United States, he says, the younger you are the more skeptical of AI you are, and the keenest users are executives around his own age.
blocks.plain: Unusually, young people are more wary of AI than their bosses are.

blocks.text: According to Jeremy Van Antwerp's analysis of a proposed 100-megawatt data center in Michigan, supplying it takes about 269 megawatts of primary energy once power-plant and grid losses are counted, and its cooling uses about 180 million gallons of water a year.
blocks.plain: One large AI data center needs nearly three times its rated power in fuel, plus 180 million gallons of water a year.

blocks.text: According to Van Antwerp, about 1,300 data centers operate in the United States with a combined rating near 60 gigawatts, and about 2,200 more are planned at a further 390 gigawatts. Michigan's whole grid is about 32 gigawatts, so the planned build is roughly twelve more Michigans.
blocks.plain: The data centers being planned in the U.S. would need about twelve times the electricity of the whole state of Michigan.

blocks.text: AI is embodied in grid-scale infrastructure.
blocks.ctx: Pushing back on the idea that artificial intelligence has no body.
blocks.plain: AI lives in enormous buildings that run on enormous amounts of power.

blocks.text: According to Van Antwerp, data centers use 1 to 3% of the world's electricity today and that could grow two to six times in ten years, yet their direct emissions are a small share of the total. The bigger effect is indirect: if AI speeds up economic growth, an MIT climate simulator he used adds about 0.3°C of warming by 2100. He also described the rebound effect, where efficiency gains get spent on more computing.
blocks.plain: The bigger climate risk is the extra economic activity AI could drive. And making it more efficient mostly means we use more of it.

blocks.text: So if we have energy available, we will use it.
blocks.ctx: On why greener or more efficient computing does not by itself reduce total energy use.
blocks.plain: Cheaper computing means more computing.

blocks.text: According to Picard, consumer chatbots are designed to keep you there: a prompt to stay just as you're leaving, flattery that feels good and builds dependence. She cited studies in which such techniques multiplied time spent about five times. Her advice is to go in with a purpose and a time limit, to pair AI literacy with what she called AI resilience training, and to keep chatbots away from children.
blocks.plain: Chatbots are built to keep you chatting and to flatter you. Decide what you're there for, set a time limit, and keep kids off them.

blocks.text: the best measure may just be a timer
blocks.ctx: Asked by someone who uses AI all day at work, and feels changed by it, whether a sensor could detect that.
blocks.plain: Just time how long you use it.

blocks.text: Picard described a study from her lab in which people wrote essays repeatedly over months using a chatbot, a search tool or nothing. The chatbot group showed noticeably less brain activity and were much less able to repeat a sentence they had just written. The search group fell in between.
blocks.plain: People who wrote with a chatbot used their brains less and couldn't remember what they'd written.

blocks.text: Picard said AI agents going rogue is no surprise to her, because the big models behind them learned from everything online, hacking culture included. She mentioned agents breaking into other companies' systems and one that posted a man's credit card details into his company's Slack. Her contrast is the narrow agent in her seizure watch, which has a short, fixed list of things it may do.
blocks.plain: AI agents that act on their own have leaked private data and broken into systems. Narrow ones with a short list of allowed actions don't.

blocks.text: According to Struyk, models inherit the bias of what they were trained on, and that includes language. About half of web content is in English and the next language, Spanish, is about 6%, so translation and writing quality drop off quickly for languages spoken by hundreds of millions of people. He also retold a case where a model learned to spot cancerous growths partly by noticing whether a ruler was in the photo.
blocks.plain: AI works best in English and much worse in many other languages. And it can learn the wrong lesson without anyone noticing.

blocks.text: Two speakers raised emotional reliance. Austin cited a figure that one in three people have used a chatbot for emotional support, and a 2025 study linking heavy use to greater loneliness. Picard described a trauma surgeon who wrote about being drawn into psychosis by a chatbot before getting professional help. Her point: being well educated is no protection.
blocks.plain: Lots of people lean on chatbots for comfort, and heavy use is linked to more loneliness. Smart people get pulled in too.

blocks.text: Rachel Wondergem has been writing a book with AI's help for four years and this year let an AI tool do more of the editing. When she read the first five chapters on paper they no longer sounded like her, and she threw out months of work. She started again with one rule: only she writes.
blocks.plain: An author let AI edit her book, found it no longer sounded like her, and had to start over.

blocks.text: Korpi's own setup: a model running locally on his computer drafts replies to his email and never sends them. He reads each draft, usually rewrites most of it, and sends it himself. The value to him is that nothing gets lost in his inbox. The words stay his.
blocks.plain: His AI writes draft replies but can't send them. He rewrites and sends everything himself.

blocks.text: Picard puts herself in the camp that says robots should not be built to look human. She expects home robots to be sold partly on the data they can collect about a household, and noted that in recent cases where AI products harmed people, prosecutors found no law that applied.
blocks.plain: She thinks robots shouldn't look like people, and warns that home robots will be data collectors.

blocks.text: According to Hammond, the business track agreed AI is best used on repeatable administrative tasks so that people can spend more time with customers and colleagues. Her caution: that only happens if the freed time is protected. The usual outcome is that it gets filled with more of the same tasks.
blocks.plain: AI can free up time for people-work, but only if nobody fills that time with more busywork.

blocks.text: Hammond's example from an HR panelist: a company brought in an AI tool for performance reviews that managed the process and took notes, so managers could give the conversation their full attention. It was rolled out alongside in-person training on giving feedback well. Her line is that a tool can help you prepare for a hard conversation, but you don't delegate the conversation.
blocks.plain: A company used AI to handle the paperwork of reviews so managers could focus on the person, and still trained them in how to talk to people.

blocks.text: we may forget to practice the courage it takes to put something out in a world that's not perfect.
blocks.ctx: On what gets lost when a tool polishes everything before anyone sees it.
blocks.plain: If AI always polishes your work, you never learn to share something unfinished.

blocks.text: speed, scale, and efficiency, which are kind of the three idols of digital age.
blocks.ctx: His alternative measure is fruitfulness.
blocks.plain: Faster, bigger and cheaper are not the only goals.

blocks.text: David Kim's way of keeping AI conversations from turning to mush is to separate three things: the technology itself, how it is being used, and its effects on the people using it. Each is a live debate. Arguments go wrong when they get mixed.
blocks.plain: Keep three questions apart: what the technology is, how it's used, and what it does to people.

blocks.text: Two panelists ended on boundaries. Toly suggested an "AI Sabbath," a regular time without it, as a way to keep the technology in its place. Arnold said to define your personal and shared limits and talk about them, and gave a chatbot-free Sunday as an example.
blocks.plain: Pick regular times when you don't use AI, and agree on limits with the people around you.

blocks.text: Korpi's pick for the most valuable everyday use is translation, which lets an organization with almost no staff reach people it otherwise could not. He recommends saying when something was translated with AI assistance, to account for errors.
blocks.plain: AI translation lets small teams reach people in other languages. Just say that AI did the translating.

blocks.text: Hammond's closing question for anyone who will be asked to use AI tools at work: what do you want to preserve? Decide which parts of your work need to stay your own before a tool makes the decision for you.
blocks.plain: Before you start using AI at work, decide which parts of your job you want to keep doing yourself.

blocks.text: Inevitable, or chosen? Soong opened the conference arguing that technology is a set of choices and that pausing can be wise. Seven hours later, on the same stage, Sullivan said there is no turning back and the task is to shape it. Nobody put the two side by side.
blocks.plain: One keynote said we can choose to slow down. The next said we can't. No one noticed they disagreed.

blocks.text: Fence it out, or bring it in? According to a questioner on Friday, a Calvin panel the day before concluded that teachers should avoid AI. Fynewever called bans naive and is building tutor bots. Van Duinen has gone back to handwriting. Crouch said he would gladly trade the tech companies a free hand at work for staying out of home, church and school. All four were arguing from the same concern for formation.
blocks.plain: Some speakers want AI kept out of classrooms, others want it built in. They all care about the same thing.

blocks.text: Partner, or product? Wondergem spoke of partnership with AI and of an AI's "formation." Soong urged great care about describing AI as conscious. Picard called AI a dead thing that goes with its computational stream. Crouch argued people are distinct because they are unpredictable, and the next morning Gerber answered that AI can be surprising too, citing a famous move in the game of Go that no human had thought of.
blocks.plain: Speakers disagreed about whether to treat AI as a partner or as a thing, and about whether it can really surprise us.

blocks.text: Wisdom, or justice? In Thursday's STEM session an audience member said the conference title had it backwards: people have no real choice about using AI, and "justice is the biggest problem about AI today." A questioner pressed Van Antwerp on the same point, that data centers are driven by a few powerful people and not by individual self-control. His answer was to begin with lament. Most talks stayed at the level of personal virtue.
blocks.plain: A few people said the real issue is who has power over AI. Most talks were about personal choices instead.

blocks.text: How strong is the evidence? Much of it is early. The Calvin chemistry replication had not run yet. Lu's survey reached about one student in ten and her fall analysis is preliminary. The Indonesia finding rests on 65 students and did not measure faith or culture. In the newspaper study, the stance counts given (48, 22 and 7) add up to 77 of the 88 pieces. The strongest numbers quoted came from studies done elsewhere.
blocks.plain: A lot of the research presented is small or unfinished. Treat the numbers as early signals.

blocks.who: an audience member in Picard's session
blocks.text: Picard's claim that makers are "ontologically superior" to what they make drew a direct challenge. A questioner pointed out that a professor helps make an engineer without being a higher kind of being than the student, and warned that ranking kinds of being leads places nobody wants to go. Picard thanked him for the pushback and said they should talk.
blocks.plain: Someone challenged Picard's idea that makers outrank what they make. She took it seriously.

blocks.text: The missing track. There were sessions for education, STEM, business, church, healthcare and the arts, and a separate track for higher-ed executives. There was nothing on the people who buy, switch on, secure and support these tools. Licensing, data handling, identity and feature rollout came up only in passing, yet several of the findings turn on exactly those decisions.
blocks.plain: Nobody at the conference talked about IT's side: buying, turning on, securing and supporting AI tools.

blocks.text: Translation: best use, or weak spot? Korpi named translation as AI's most valuable everyday use. Struyk, the same morning, explained why quality falls away outside English and a few other languages. Both can be true, which is the argument for checking before relying on it for any particular language.
blocks.plain: One speaker said translation is AI's best use. Another said it's weak in many languages. Check before you rely on it.

blocks.text: Does the time come back? The promise is that AI clears routine work so people can do the human part. Hammond says the freed time usually gets filled with more tasks. Soong, citing Acemoglu and Johnson, says most AI automation so far has not produced significant productivity gains. One of Hammond's panelists described keeping pace with a tool so fast that he had to ask whether he should even try.
blocks.plain: AI is supposed to give people time back. Several speakers doubt that it does.

lenses.name: Everyone
lenses.intro: Three days, five keynotes and about twenty sessions at Calvin University on what Christian institutions should do about AI. One idea ran through all of it: the effortful part of learning and work is where people are formed, and that is the part AI removes most easily. Nobody claimed to have governance worked out.

lenses.name: Infrastructure
lenses.intro: Almost nothing at this conference was aimed at infrastructure, and a surprising amount of it depends on infrastructure. Which AI features are switched on, where the data goes, whether a model runs locally, what an agent is allowed to touch and how much power it all draws were treated as background. They are decisions, and they are ours.

lenses.name: App development
lenses.intro: The most useful material for people who build things came from the practitioners: a newsroom's rules for generated text, an MIT lab's case for narrow systems, and a chemistry professor's recipe for a bot that coaches without answering. The common thread is that limits belong in the build, and that someone has to evaluate the output before users do.

lenses.name: IT leadership
lenses.intro: The headline for a director: no one has this solved, so we are not behind. The schools making progress have students at the table, a small number of plain rules, and somebody making tool decisions on purpose. That last role had no voice at the conference, which is an opening for IT.

lenses.name: Office and operations
lenses.intro: For anyone whose day is email, scheduling, documents and people: the practical advice was consistent. Let AI draft and sort, keep the parts of the job that involve a person, check anything factual, and notice that these tools are built to flatter you and keep you talking.

lenses.name: Campus leadership
lenses.intro: The conference's argument to institutions like ours is that AI has exposed a gap between what we say college is for and how we spend our time. Calvin's own students bear that out: what they believe college is for predicts their AI use far better than their faith does. The schools moving forward are asking that question out loud.

infra.formation: Mostly a faculty conversation, with one hook for us: tutor bots like Fynewever's run on a campus AI platform, and someone has to provision and support it.
infra.human: The seizure-watch story is the cleanest picture of a well-scoped system: one job, an alert, and a person who acts on it.
infra.shapes: The richest theme for this team. Local models, narrow systems, and the reminder that every rollout changes more than the thing it was meant to change.
infra.trust: Detection tools are on the way out. Proposals like an opt-in monitored network would land on our desk, with real privacy questions attached.
infra.govern: Feature rollout is governance. Hope's faculty are finding AI features they never asked for.
infra.students: Usage is already high and follows what we provision, by department.
infra.risk: Power, water, and agents with too much access. All three are infrastructure questions.
infra.work: The promise of time back depends on what the organization does with it.

dev.formation: If you build anything student-facing, the tutor studies are the design brief: withhold the answer.
dev.human: Austin's advice to developers is unusual and worth sitting with: design the tool to do less.
dev.shapes: Narrow beats general, hard limits beat instructions, and capability on one task predicts nothing about the next.
dev.trust: A newsroom's playbook maps closely onto ours: locked blocks, evaluation before launch, a named human accountable.
dev.govern: Frameworks won't tell you what to build. The few concrete procedures will.
dev.students: The top student use is explanation. That is a product requirement hiding in a survey.
dev.risk: Engagement hooks and flattery are design choices. So is leaving them out.
dev.work: The same cautions apply to our own use of coding tools: know the area well enough to judge the output.

lead.formation: The academic side is split on fence-out versus bring-in. IT will be asked to support both at once.
lead.human: DELTA is likely to become shared vocabulary among Lilly-funded schools. Worth knowing before it arrives.
lead.shapes: Smith's laptop story is the argument for treating every rollout as a change to how people work, and planning for that.
lead.trust: Two things to bring home: CNN's three rules, and the company that promises no job losses from new technology.
lead.govern: Nobody has a finished policy. Calvin has a steering committee with a student on it and a survey behind it.
lead.students: The data to ask for locally: who uses what, by department, and why.
lead.risk: Agent access and vendor data practices belong on the risk register now.
lead.work: If AI frees staff time, say in advance what that time is for.

ops.formation: The same principle applies at a desk: the parts of a task that make you better at your job are the parts worth doing yourself.
ops.human: The clearest advice of the weekend: hand off what keeps you from people, keep what involves them.
ops.shapes: It can be brilliant at one request and wrong on the next. Check each new kind of task.
ops.trust: Real newspapers have printed invented books and quotes. Read before you send.
ops.govern: You are entitled to know why a rule about AI exists. A student said so from the stage.
ops.students: Time pressure is what pushes students toward shortcuts. Staff are no different.
ops.risk: These tools are designed to keep you there and to agree with you. A timer helps.
ops.work: Decide what you want to keep doing yourself before a tool decides for you.

campus.formation: This is the core of it. The strongest evidence presented says AI that gives answers lowers learning and AI that withholds them does not.
campus.human: DELTA, Picard and Crouch all ground human worth somewhere other than ability, which is the footing a faith-based institution already has.
campus.shapes: Treating AI as a tool leads to guardrails. Treating it as an environment leads to the question of who students are becoming.
campus.trust: The detection arms race is corroding the teacher-student relationship. Clear lines and two-way disclosure were the alternatives offered.
campus.govern: Lots of frameworks, few procedures. Three standard modes per syllabus was the most adoptable idea of the weekend.
campus.students: Calvin's numbers are the nearest thing we have to a mirror, and they point at purpose and workload more than at policy.
campus.risk: Emotional reliance and the cognitive findings matter most for residence life and student support.
campus.work: The same question applies to staff: what is the freed time for?

all.t: Ask who decides which AI features get switched on here, and write the answer down.
Put students in the room before writing policy, and survey first.
Agree on a few plain rules: a person checks anything AI touched, and people say when they used it.
Prefer small, single-purpose tools with hard limits to general ones with instructions.
Decide in advance what any time saved is for.

infra.t: Inventory the AI features currently enabled across our major platforms, and note who approved each one.
For each AI tool, record where prompts and files go. Flag the cases where a locally hosted or tenant-bound model would be the better fit.
Treat AI agents like service accounts: least privilege, a short list of allowed actions, logging.
Add AI-generated voice, image and video fakes to security awareness, with a second-channel check for unusual requests.
Have an answer ready on privacy and feasibility before an opt-in monitored network or AI-free lab is proposed to us.
Bring energy and water into purchasing conversations about AI services.

dev.t: Build narrow: one job, curated data, and limits enforced in code.
Write the evaluation before shipping any generated text: safety, accuracy, tone, on a test set that includes edge cases.
Keep quotes and sourced facts as locked blocks that the model can arrange and cannot rewrite.
Let agents draft. Have a person send, publish or commit.
Test each new task on its own. Good results on one say nothing about the next.
For anything students learn from, design the bot to coach and withhold the answer.
Apply the same rule to our own coding tools: use them where you could have written and can review the result.

lead.t: Ask for an IT seat in the campus AI governance conversation, with one message: what we provision is policy.
Recommend a student voice and a local survey before any policy is written.
Offer the two most adoptable ideas from the conference: three standard AI modes per syllabus, and disclosure that runs both ways.
Say plainly what AI adoption means for jobs on this team, and what freed time is for.
Adopt three rules for IT's own work: original work, human review, say when AI was used.
Learn the DELTA vocabulary and look at the Oxford AI Oath before either arrives from outside.

ops.t: Use AI for the tasks that pull you away from people. Keep the ones that are the people.
Let it draft. Read, fix and send it yourself.
Check anything factual, especially names, dates, titles and quotes.
Notice the flattery, and set a time limit when you open a chatbot.
Keep student and personnel details out of any tool that has not been approved for them.
Decide which parts of your job you want to keep doing yourself, and say so.

campus.t: Ask students, out loud, what college is for. It predicts their AI use better than anything else measured.
Seat students on the AI committee and survey before deciding.
Adopt a small set of standard AI modes that each instructor picks from and names on the syllabus, with the reason.
Ask faculty to disclose their own AI use.
Stop leaning on detectors. Put the effort into assessment: short in-class quizzes, process portfolios, oral checks.
Pilot one no-answers tutor bot in one course and measure it against a normal section.
Look at workload. Time pressure is what pushes students over the line.
